questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: A man presents with a slowly progressive swelling over the past 1 and 1/2 years. On examination, it has a variable consistency and appears as shown in the image. What is the probable cause?
questions.explanation:
A slowly progressive swelling, with a variable consistency, lifting the ear lobe, is suggestive of pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland.

Pleomorphic adenoma, the most common benign salivary gland tumor, primarily affects the parotid gland, particularly its superficial lobe. It is also referred to as a mixed tumor due to its combination of epithelial and mesenchymal components. This tumor most commonly occurs in females around the age of 40.

Clinical features:

  • Painless, slow-growing swelling
  • Lobulated, firm, variable in consistency
  • Lifts the earlobe
  • No facial nerve involvement
  • Curtain sign positive - cannot be moved above the zygomatic bone.
  • In case of deep lobe involvement, tonsils, and faucial pillars will be pushed medially.
  • Features of malignancy - a sudden increase in size, ulceration of the overlying skin, facial nerve palsy (involvement of facial nerve), painful swelling, and restriction of jaw movements.

Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is the investigation of choice in diagnosing pleomorphic adenoma. Open biopsy is contraindicated due to the chances of injury to the facial nerve.

All tumors of the superficial lobe of the parotid gland should be managed by superficial parotidectomy. Radical parotidectomy is performed for malignant pleomorphic adenoma.

Other options:

Option A: Adamantinoma is a low-grade malignant tumor that usually presents with pre-tibial pain and swelling since it most commonly affects the tibial diaphysis.

Option B:  Dermoid cysts present as firm painless subcutaneous nodules and are of 4 types:

  1. Sequestration dermoid - sequestration of epithelium during embryological development.
  2. Tubulodermoid - accumulation of secretions from ectodermal tube/duct
  3. Implantation dermoid - implantation of the epidermis due to trauma
  4. Teratomatous dermoid - having all 3 germ layers (ecto, meso, and endoderm)

Option D: Sebaceous cysts are retention cysts of the sebaceous glands that present as smooth, non-tender, non-transillumination swelling with a punctum (in 70% of the patients).

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: What is shown in the given image?
questions.explanation:
The image shows a dark-colored summit over a swelling, usually seen in a sebaceous cyst.

Sebaceous cysts are the retention cysts of the sebaceous gland that are usually present on the face, scalp, or scrotum. They contain yellowish-white cheesy material with fat and epithelium.

Clinical features: 

  • The swelling is painless, soft, and freely mobile.
  • Though non-transilluminating, they are Paget's test positive (fluctuant).
  • Punctum is seen in 70% of the patients with sebaceous cysts. They are dark in color due to the accumulation of denuded epithelium.
  • They also have an unpleasant sebum odor.
  • The swelling can ulcerate and become painful (Cock’s peculiar tumor).
  • Some cysts over the scalp may also harden over time (Sebaceous horn).
  • Many may get infected and lead to abscess formation.

Treatment:

  • Excision including skin adjacent to punctum using elliptical incision-dissection method.
  • Incision and avulsion of cyst wall.
  • In the presence of an abscess, an initial treatment with an incision later followed by excision of the cyst

Other options:

Option A: Dermoid cysts present as firm painless subcutaneous nodules and are of 4 types:

  1. Sequestration dermoid - sequestration of epithelium during embryological development
  2. Tubulodermoid - accumulation of secretions from ectodermal tube/duct
  3. Implantation dermoid - implantation of the epidermis due to trauma
  4. Teratomatous dermoid - having all 3 germ layers (ecto, meso, and endoderm)

Option C: Meningiomas are benign tumors arising from the meningothelial cells of the dura. They present with headaches, seizures, or focal neurological deficits.

Option D: Postauricular cutaneous mastoid fistula is a rare complication of chronic otitis media that heals very slowly and needs surgical closure.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: A female patient presents with a breast abscess. An aspiration was attempted under antibiotic cover which failed to reveal any aspirate. What is the next step in management?
options: Stop antibiotics as no aspirate was collected
questions.explanation:
In a patient with a breast abscess, the next step after a failed aspiration is to attempt aspiration once again under antibiotic cover.

Incision and drainage is not preferred, as it can potentially interfere with breastfeeding, and delicate structures such as ducts, lobules, and tubules may be injured, possibly leading to a non-healing milk fistula.

A breast abscess is a complication of acute mastitis, which is more common in new mothers at the beginning of lactation (lactational mastitis). Non-lactational mastitis is more common in diabetic, immunosuppressed people and people predisposed by duct ectasia and periareolar infections.

Clinical features of a breast abscess include:

  • Fever and malaise
  • Localized pain and tenderness 
  • Redness and swelling of the affected breast
  • Positive fluctuation test.


An ultrasonogram of the affected breast is performed to confirm the abscess, and treatment proceeds as follows:

  • Analgesics, antipyretics, and breast support for pain and fever relief.
  • Aspiration is performed under antibiotic cover, and the pus is cultured. If aspiration proves unsuccessful, it should be reattempted after a few days.
  • Incision and drainage should be considered in cases of:
    • Mastitis unresponsive to antibiotics for 48 hours.
    • Brawny induration.
    • Progressive mastitis with persistent fever

Note:

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: Which nerve is involved in Frey’s syndrome?
questions.explanation:
The auriculotemporal nerve (V3 nerve) is involved in Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating).

Frey’s syndrome is also known as Dupuy syndrome or auriculotemporal syndrome. It commonly develops after parotid surgery. It is caused by an aberrant regeneration of post-ganglionic parasympathetic nerve fibers crossed along the sympathetic pathways to the sweat glands near the parotid region.

Clinical features are due to the result of salivary stimulation (by the smell or taste of food) leading to the sweating and flushing of the periauricular region on the involved side of the face. A starch iodine test is used for diagnosis.

Treatment ranges from antiperspirants (in mild cases) to tympanic neurectomy or botulinum toxin injection (in severe cases). It can be prevented by incorporating careful extracapsular dissection and closure of the superficial musculoaponeurotic layer during parotidectomy.



Other options:

Option A: Facial nerve is the 7th cranial nerve that supplies the muscles of the face, and results in facial paralysis if injured during parotidectomy

Option B: Oculomotor is the 3rd cranial nerve which supplies the extraocular muscles. If injured during ophthalmic surgeries, it results in ocular paralysis and the eye pointing down and out.

Option D: Glossopharyngeal nerve is the 9th cranial nerve and its injury causes loss of taste sensation from the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding deep vein thrombosis (DVT)?
options: Most common clinical presentation is pain and tenderness in calf
Some cases may directly present as pulmonary thromboembolism
questions.explanation:
Most cases of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) are unilateral. It is bilateral in only 30% of the individuals.

DVT refers to thrombosis of the deep venous system.

Caused by:

  • Postoperative thrombosis (most common cause)
  • Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs)
  • After childbirth
  • Immobility 

Sites:

  • Pelvic veins—common
  • Leg veins—common in femoral and popliteal veins (common on the left side).

Fever is the earliest symptom, which is also most commonly accompanied by pain and tenderness in the calf and thigh (option C).

The following signs could be elicited:

  • Positive Homan's sign: Resistance of calf muscles on passive foreceful dorsiflexion of the foot.
  • Mose's sign: Gentle squeezing of the lower part of the calf from side to side is painful.
  • Neuhof's sign: Thickening and deep tenderness seen on deep palpation of the calf muscles.

Sometimes, the thrombus may get dislodged and present as pulmonary thromboembolism (option D) with features of dyspnoea, tachypnoea, and chest pain.

Clinical features are unreliable for making a definitive diagnosis (option A), and a venous Doppler is the best modality for confirming DVT. It reveals a non-compressible dilated vein. The likelihood of pulmonary embolism can be predicted using modified Wells criteria.

Patients with DVT should be immediately started with subcutaneous low molecular weight heparin (LMWH). If contraindicated due to renal insufficiency or thrombocytopenia-related conditions, they should be started on fondaparinux (indirect factor Xa inhibitor) or bivalirudin (direct thrombin inhibitor). Anticoagulants should be administered for a minimum period of 3 months. Vena cava filters are used in patients with bleeding risks (like hemophilia).

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding rectal carcinoma?
options: Hartmann’s operation is done in elderly debilitated patients
Adenocarcinoma is a rare variant of rectal carcinoma
Early morning spurious diarrhoea and tenesmus can occur
Growth confined to the rectal mucosa is stage A of modified Duke’s staging
questions.correct_answer: Adenocarcinoma is a rare variant of rectal carcinoma
questions.explanation:
Adenocarcinoma is the most common variant of rectal carcinoma.

Colorectal cancer is:

  1. The second most common malignancy globally
  2. The second most common cancer in women
  3. The third most common cancer in men
  4. The fourth most common cause of death due to cancer. 

Symptoms of rectal carcinoma include:

  1. Painless bleeding - earliest and most common
  2. Alteration of bowel habits - change in frequency and consistency of the stool
  3. Tenesmus - unable to pass a motion even when there is the sensation of needing to evacuate the bowel. It is suggestive of a tumor of the lower half of the rectum 
  4. Early morning bloody diarrhea (option C) - passage of blood and mucus in addition to feces. Pain and weight loss are usually late symptoms

Abdominal examination and digital rectal examination are used for the primary evaluation. Rigid sigmoidoscopy is performed to obtain a biopsy. A synchronous tumor (primary tumor with a different origin than the one currently investigated) is excluded by performing a colonoscopy.

Modified Duke’s classification:

A

Growth limited up to the rectal mucosa (option D)

B

B1: Tumor invading muscularis propria, no lymph node invasion.

B2: Tumors invading into or through serosa, no lymph node invasion.

C

C1: The tumour did not exceed the bowel wall, lymph node metastasis.

C2: Tumour exceeded the intestinal wall and lymph node metastasis.

D

Distant metastasis


Surgery is the mainstay of management for rectal carcinoma. Non-operative management is offered to only those patients who have a complete clinical response to neoadjuvant.

The type of surgery depends on multiple factors (size, location, age of the patient, etc). However, the general consensus is:

  1. Early cancer (T1 and a few T2) is locally excised via the transanal approach.
  2. Most rectal cancer is treated by anterior resection and colorectal/coloanal anastomosis.
  3. Low extensive tumors are treated by laparoscopic abdominoperineal resection(APR) and permanent colostomy.
  4. Hartmann’s operation (option A) is preferred in old and frail patients due to poor anal sphincter and postoperative incontinence.

A gasless abdomen is an X-ray feature that can be seen in acute pancreatitis. Patients with acute pancreatitis can have significant vomiting and diarrhea that may produce a gasless abdomen.

  • A paucity of small bowel gas may be a normal finding in some adults

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: Gall stone chemistry most commonly seen amongst the following is:
questions.explanation:
The most common gallstone chemistry seen is crystalline cholesterol monohydrate.

Types of gallstones:

  1. Cholesterol stones (75% of gallstones) have >70% cholesterol by weight and are composed of crystalline cholesterol monohydrate. The majority of cholesterol stones have a mixed composition with bile pigments and calcium, in addition to the cholesterol. They are the most common type of gall stones worldwide and in India.
  2. Pigment stones have <20% cholesterol and are dark due to the presence of calcium bilirubinate as the major constituent.
    1. Black pigment stones (20% of gallstones) - are formed due to supersaturation of unconjugated bilirubin (seen in hereditary hemolytic anemia (like sickle cell and hereditary spherocytosis)
    2. Brown pigment stones (5% of gallstones) - formed secondary to infections (like E. coli, and Ascaris lumbricoides)

Note: Pure cholesterol stones are uncommon and account for <10% of all stones.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: Which of the following are indications for surgical intervention in abdominal aortic aneurysms?
options: Size more than 5.5 cm in males
Size more than 5 cm in females
questions.explanation:
All the given are indications for surgical intervention in abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). The indications include:

  • Size >5.5 cm in males (option A)
  • Size >4.5-5 cm in females (option B)
  • Expansion of >0.5 cm within 6 months or >1 cm in one year (option C)
  • Painful, tender aneurysm 
  • Thrombosed aneurysm, aneurysm with distal emboli 

The rupture risk is high for aneurysms >5.5 cm and begins to rise exponentially with an increase in size. Women are at higher risk for rupture than men, with a lower threshold of 4.5 to 5.0 cm (depending on the reference used).

Screening is done for:

  • Cardiovascular patients in men and women (60-85 years)
  • Men and women >50 years with positive family history 
  • Annual screening in asymptomatic patients with 4-4.5 cm size, size >4.5 cm once in every 6 months.

Management of AAA can be done by open repair or endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR). About 75% of infrarenal aneurysms are suitable for endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR), depending on the morphology of the aneurysm assessed by a CT scan.

Aneurysms that fall below the mentioned indications may safely be followed with CT or ultrasound at 6-month intervals since long-term outcomes to routine follow-up are equivalent to earlier surgical repair of the aneurysm. Smoking cessation is very important and reduces the mortality rate.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: The following image shows the retrograde ureteropyelogram of a patient with loin pain. What is the most probable clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given image showing dilated clubbed calyces with stricture of the left ureteropelvic junction points to a diagnosis of hydronephrosis.

Hydronephrosis refers to the dilatation of the pelvicalyceal system caused by a partial or complete blockage of urinary flow. 

Investigations:

  • Ultrasound is the least invasive technique for diagnosing hydronephrosis.
  • Retrograde pyelography is rarely indicated but will confirm the site of obstruction before corrective surgery.
  • Intravenous urogram (IVU) is helpful only if the obstructed kidney is functional. In IVU, the extrarenal pelvis is dilated and the minor calyces lose their normal cupping. In early stages, there is blunting of calyces followed by its clubbing in the late stages.
  • A renal isotope scan (DTPA or MAG-3) is the best modality to confirm the obstructive dilatation of the collecting system.

questions.question: Which of the following types of renal stones are produced by laxative abuse?
questions.explanation:
Ammonium urate stones are most likely to be seen in patients with laxative abuse.

Loss of potassium and sodium in laxative abuse causes intracellular acidosis, which increases the production of ammonia in urine. Dehydration and sodium loss further exacerbate hypokalemia and reduces the urinary volume, resulting in hyperuricemia. Highly concentrated uric acid and ammonia promote the formation of ammonium urate stones.

These are also associated with inflammatory bowel disease, chronic diarrhea, ileostomy, recurrent urinary tract infection and recurrent uric acid stone formation.

  • The score for eye-opening: 2, because his eyes are opening to only painful stimuli.
  • The score for best motor response: 5, because he can localize pain.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: A patient presents with a painless swelling of the neck. The histology of the tissue is as given in the image below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The slide shows the histopathology of Hashimoto thyroiditis, with:

  • Follicular destruction
  • Reduced colloid with increased interstitial connective tissue
  • Small lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltration
  • A well-developed germinal centre may be seen
  • Hurthle (Askanazy) cells that have abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm lining the follicles


Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas. It is also known as struma lymphomatosa or lymphocytic thyroiditis. It is an autoimmune disease that results in the destruction of the thyroid gland and gradual & progressive thyroid failure.

Clinical features:

  • Most prevalent between 45-65 years of age
  • More common in females
  • Painless enlargement of the thyroid
  • Hashitoxicosis: When the auto-antibodies attack and damage the follicles, there is a sudden release of thyroid hormones from these follicles. This leads to a transient phase of thyrotoxicosis.
  • Hypothyroidism: Since the follicles are damaged and cannot form the hormones anymore, these patients tend to be in a state of hypothyroidism.

Diagnosis:

  • T3 and T4 are low
  • TSH is raised
  • Autoantibodies against:
    • Thyroid receptors
    • Thyroid peroxidase (TPO)
    • Thyroglobulin

These patients are managed with thyroid hormone replacement therapy.

In patients with long-standing goiter, there is a risk of compressive features and the development of thyroid lymphoma. Such cases can be treated with total thyroidectomy. It may also predispose to papillary thyroid carcinoma.

Other options: 

Option A: Histological features of medullary carcinoma of the thyroid include polygonal to spindle-shaped cells in the form of nests, trabeculae or follicles. Small, round anaplastic cells may be found in some cases and amyloid deposits derived from calcitonin polypeptides are present in the stroma.

The given slide below shows medullary carcinoma of thyroid:



Option C: Grave's disease is an autoimmune disorder characterized by hyperthyroidism due to circulating autoantibodies. The thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins bind to the TSH receptors, causing overgrowth of the thyroid gland and increased thyroid hormone synthesis. Histologically, there is acinar cell hypertrophy and hyperplasia with the absence of normal colloid in the tall columnar epithelium (normally the epithelium is flat with colloid). Lymphoid infiltrates, consisting predominantly of T cells, along with scattered B cells and mature plasma cells, are present throughout the interstitium. Germinal centers are common.

The given slide below shows Grave's disease:

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: A 45-year-old male patient who presented with a scrotal swelling underwent an orchidectomy. The image below shows the histopathology findings. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Based on the gross and microscopic appearance of the specimen, the diagnosis is seminoma.

The gross specimen shows a well-circumscribed, pale, gray-white, fleshy, homogenous mass, with a lobulated cut surface, usually devoid of hemorrhage or necrosis. Histopathology shows uniform tumor cells with abundant clear cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and large central nuclei. There is a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate. Classically, they have a fried egg appearance.

Other options:

Option B: Yolk-sac tumor has a yellowish-white, mucinous appearance. Histologically, they are typically composed of a lace-like (reticular) network of medium-sized cuboidal, flattened, or spindled cells, which generally show less cytologic atypia than embryonal carcinoma. In approximately 50% of tumors, structures resembling endodermal sinuses (Schiller-Duval bodies) may be seen; these consist of a mesodermal core with a central capillary and a visceral and parietal layer of cells resembling primitive glomeruli. 



Option C: Embryonal cell carcinoma appears variegated with foci of hemorrhage or necrosis.  Histologically, the cells grow in alveolar or tubular patterns, sometimes with papillary folds. More undifferentiated lesions may display sheets of cells with cleft-like spaces. The neoplastic cells have an epithelial appearance, are large and anaplastic, and have hyperchromatic nuclei with prominent nucleoli. The cell borders are usually indistinct, and there is considerable variation in cell and nuclear size and shape (pleomorphism). Mitotic figures and tumor giant cells are frequently seen.



Option D: Teratomas also have a variegated appearance but have cysts reflecting the multiplicity of tissue types. Histologically, collections of differentiated cells or organoid structures originating in all 3 germ layers can be seen. Elements may be mature (resembling various adult tissues) or immature (sharing histologic features with fetal or embryonic tissue).

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: A surgeon sees a necrotic bowel when operating on a child for an inguinal hernia. What is true about the resection and anastomosis of the bowel?
options: The surgeon must use chromic catgut
The surgeon must not include the submucosa in the sutures
The surgeon must use the single-layer, extramucosal suture technique
The surgeon must use the single-layer seromuscular suture technique
questions.correct_answer: The surgeon must use the single-layer, extramucosal suture technique
questions.explanation:
The standard technique used currently for resection anastomosis of the bowel is a one-layer extra mucosal suture technique since it causes the least tissue necrosis and luminal narrowing. Interrupted and continuous single-layer suture techniques are adequate and safe.

The extra mucosal suture must also include the submucosa because this layer has a high collagen content and it is the most stable suture layer in all sections of the gastrointestinal tract.

Catgut has now been replaced with absorbable synthetic polymers. Stapling devices can be used when speed is required.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: A lady comes with a reddish firm nodule on her chest which hasn't grown in size. Its histolopathological image is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of a woman with reddish firm nodule on her chest and histology showing multiple dilated vascular structures with a single layer of epithelial cells is suggestive of a hemangioma.

Hemangioma is a benign tumor caused by the abnormal growth of blood vessels. Types of hemangioma are capillary hemangioma (most common), juvenile/ strawberry hemangioma, cavernous hemangioma and pyogenic hemangioma.

Indications for immediate treatment are complications such as ulceration or those pertaining to the location of the mass (e.g. visual issues due to a large hemangioma over the eyelid).

Treatment options include:

  • Beta-blockers - oral propranolol
  • Steroids - intralesional triamcinolone, topical clobetasol, systemic steroids
  • Interferon alfa-2a and vincristine - for steroid-resistant lesions
  • Local resection with cutting cautery or carbon dioxide laser

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: Which is the most common organism causing acute bacterial prostatitis?
questions.explanation:
The most common organism causing acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) is Escherichia coli.

It is commonly caused by an ascending urethral infection or reflux of infected urine into prostatic ducts. Sexually transmissible infections and other urinary pathogens, such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus faecalis may also be responsible.

The patient presents with fever, perineal pain, chills and rigor, and dysuria. Per rectal examination will reveal a tender, boggy prostate. Care should be taken to avoid aggressive palpation or prostatic massage as it can lead to bacterial dissemination and sepsis.

Urine examination and culture should be done. Urine examination reveals threads in urine.

Management:  

Patients with systemic signs of infection should be admitted for IV antibiotics, hydration, and monitoring of laboratory parameters.

Patients who have no signs of systemic infection, who can tolerate oral intake, and who have no urinary retention can be treated with oral antibiotics. Antibiotics are given for 2-6 weeks to ensure the eradication of the infection as antibiotics don't penetrate the prostate capsule easily. 

For outpatient therapy: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg oral every 12 hours or levofloxacin 500 mg OD or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double-strength tablet oral every 12 hours can be used.

For hospitalized patients: Intravenous ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin with or without an aminoglycoside (gentamicin or tobramycin) or intravenous beta-lactam with or without an aminoglycoside. Gram-positive infections are treated with cephalosporins (cephalexin, cefazolin) or dicloxacillin and vancomycin.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man came with complaints of dark-colored stools to the OPD. After undergoing endoscopy, the patient was diagnosed with an upper GI bleed. Which of the following structures is used as a demarcation point to differentiate it from a lower GI bleed?
questions.explanation:
The ligament of Treitz is used as the demarcation point to differentiate between upper gastrointestinal bleeding and lower gastrointestinal bleeding. It is a part of the duodenojejunal junction. 

Upper GI bleeding refers to bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz, and lower GI bleeding refers to bleeding distal to the ligament of Treitz.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: Which is the best graft for a femoropopliteal bypass?
questions.explanation:
The great saphenous vein (GSV) is the best as it lasts longer than polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), dacron, and human umbilical vein as a graft in a femoropopliteal bypass.

The GSV is the conduit of choice for arterial bypass grafts below the inguinal ligament.

For bypass above the inguinal ligament, while both GSV and PTFE grafts have similar patency rates in the first 2 years, the GSV is superior thereafter and hence preferred over PTFE or any other grafts.

The ipsilateral GSV is the conduit of choice for femoropopliteal bypass. When it is not available, contralateral GSV should be used. Other veins are preferred when both ipsilateral and contralateral GSV is not available and they include a small saphenous vein, cephalic vein, and basilic vein. 

Non-autogenous grafts are used for patients who lack a suitable venous conduit. The most commonly used prosthetic conduit is PTFE. Recent studies have shown that heparin-bonded PTFE is superior to compared to PTFE without heparin.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis?
questions.explanation:
Alcohol consumption is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis, accounting for 60–70% of the cases. Smoking increases the risk of alcohol-induced chronic pancreatitis.

Cystic fibrosis is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis in the pediatric age group.

Other causes of chronic pancreatitis include:
  • Pancreatic divisum
  • Annular pancreas
  • Hyperlipidemia
  • Hypercalcemia
  • Hyperparathyroidism
  • Chronic duct obstruction
  • Autoimmune pancreatitis
  • Cystic fibrosis
  • Tropical pancreatitis

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: A probe is inserted into the duct from which the nipple discharge is emerging. A tennis racquet incision is made and the flap is dissected to reach the duct. The duct is then excised.  This  procedure is known as?
options: Wide excision of the lactiferous duct.
questions.explanation:
Microdochectomy is the excision of the entire lactiferous duct (single duct disease). It is done for duct papilloma.

Microdochectomy:

  • In a duct papilloma where no palpable mass is present, the duct is expressed to observe the discharge.
  • A fine probe or stiff nylon suture is gently inserted into the duct, and the probe is secured to the nipple skin using silk sutures to prevent displacement during the procedure.
  • A tennis racquet shaped incision is made to elevate the skin flaps, and the duct with the probe is excised along with the skin flap for 5 cm until the papilloma is identified (The papilloma will always be located within 5 cm from the duct orifice).
  • The wound is closed without a drain, and a compression bandage is applied.

It is ideal to rule out DCIS by frozen section biopsy.

Cone excision and wide excision are done under major duct excision (Adair-Haldfield operation). It is done for duct ectasias with multiple duct involvement and multiple papillomas.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: Which of the following is true about chromic catgut?
options: It is made from cat gut
It is made from rabbit gut
It is absorbed by enzymatic degradation and macrophage phagocytosis
It is tanned with nickel salts to improve handling and to resist degradation in tissue
questions.correct_answer: It is absorbed by enzymatic degradation and macrophage phagocytosis
questions.explanation:
Chromic catgut is absorbed through macrophage phagocytosis and enzymatic degradation within 90 days.

It is made from collagen derived from healthy sheep or cattle. It is then tanned with chromium salts to improve handling and resist degradation in tissue.

The tensile strength lasts for 21-28 days. It has a moderate tissue reaction as compared to plain catgut, which has a high tissue reactivity.

It is used to ligate superficial vessels, suture subcutaneous tissues, and is used for stomas and other tissues that heal rapidly. It is not used in tissues that heal slowly and require prolonged support.

questions.question: Identify the instrument given in the image below:
questions.explanation:
The given image shows a Morris retractor with a single, flat transversely curved blade and a blunt projecting ridge with backward projection.

Morris retractor can be single or double-bladed. It is used to retract abdominal wall incisions, loin incisions, subcostal wounds or any wounds in depth.

It can be used to improve visibility on one side of an incision. Thus, it is valuable during the initial phase of a laparotomy.



Other options: 

Option A: Deaver's retractor is a question mark-shaped stout, atraumatic retractor with a broad, gently curved long blade. It is used to retract the abdominal wall and viscera. Moist mops should be kept underneath prior to placing this retractor. It is used for major abdominal surgeries, bladder surgeries and lumbar sympathectomy. 



Option C: Czerny's retractor is a superficial retractor with a thick and small blade on one side and a biflanged hook on the other side in opposite directions. It is used in hernia surgery and laparotomy, especially during closure.



Option D: Double-hook retractor consists of two hooks with a handle. It is used in excision of swellings like lipoma, neurofibroma and cyst. It is also used to hold the skin flaps when raising them.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: Extra mammary Paget's disease is commonly seen in the:
questions.explanation:
Extramammary Paget's disease arises most frequently on the vulva. Other sites include the perineum, scrotum, perianal skin, and penis.

Extramammary Paget's disease (EMPD) can be primary or secondary.

  • Primary EMPD is more common and occurs in the absence of an underlying malignancy, thought to arise from intraepidermal parts of apocrine glands or from pluripotent cells from the epidermis.
  • Secondary EMPD arises from an underlying adnexal carcinoma or internal malignancy due to the epidermotropic spread of malignant cells from the underlying tumor.

Visceral malignancies associated with EMPD are carcinomas of the colon, rectum, bladder, urethra, cervix, and prostate. The patient presents with well-defined, moist, erythematous scaly plaques and severe pruritis. Lichenification and excoriations may also be seen.

Diagnosis is confirmed by punch, wedge, or excisional skin biopsy. A systemic workup should also be done to identify any underlying malignancy and they include colonoscopy, cystoscopy, colposcopy, and pelvic examination with pap smear in females. 

Treatment: 

  • Mohs microscopic surgery with 5 cm margin clearance 
  • Radiotherapy 
  • Topical 5-fluorouracil and imiquimod 
  • Chemotherapy 
  • Photodynamic therapy

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: The best method to obtain tissue for the diagnosis of pancreatic carcinoma is:
options: Transgastric FNAC guided by endoscopic ultrasound
questions.correct_answer: Transgastric FNAC guided by endoscopic ultrasound
questions.explanation:
Transgastric or transduodenal FNAC or trucut biopsy performed under endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) guidance is the best method to obtain tissue for the diagnosis of pancreatic carcinoma. This is because it avoids the spillage of tumor cells into the peritoneal cavity. 

Endoscopic ultrasonography with a fine needle aspiration (EUS-FNA) is done if CT has failed to demonstrate a tumor. When a tissue diagnosis is required prior to surgery to distinguish between inflammation and neoplasia, EUS-FNA is helpful.

Diagnostic laparoscopy prior to resection can spare an unnecessary laparotomy by identifying small peritoneal and liver metastases.

Percutaneous transperitoneal biopsy of potentially resectable pancreatic tumors is avoided.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: An abdominal mass in a patient with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is best seen _________.
options: During palpation over the left hypochondrium
questions.explanation:
In a child with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS), the abdominal mass is best seen during test feed in the right upper quadrant. 

Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis most presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting. It is common between 2 and 8 weeks of age. Hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus results in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet. Male infants are at a higher risk.

Clinically, when the infant is given a test feed, an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant and visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right across the abdomen.

Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis develop a characteristic metabolic abnormality- hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Persistent vomiting results in loss of hydrochloric acid leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-).

All infants with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis are evaluated with an ultrasound (investigation of choice). It confirms the diagnosis in the majority of cases.

Management: Rehydration and metabolic correction prior to definitive surgery - Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about Crohn's disease?
options: For effective treatment of a Crohn's mass, only antibiotics are prescribed.
Symptomatic relapse after surgery is not related to the presence of disease during resection.
The proximal ileum is most commonly involved in Crohn's disease.
On endoscopic examination, continuous lesions are visualised, which are diagnostic of Crohn's disease.
questions.correct_answer: Symptomatic relapse after surgery is not related to the presence of disease during resection.
questions.explanation:
Symptomatic relapse of Crohn's disease after surgery is not related to the presence of the disease during resection. 

The course of the disease after surgery is unpredictable since surgery does not cure Crohn's disease. Instead, the probability of relapse increases with the time since resection. 

Other options:

Option A: Antibiotics alone cannot treat a Crohn's mass effectively. Abscesses can be treated with metronidazole and ciprofloxacin and should also undergo drainage (and resection if needed).

Option C: The terminal ileum is most commonly involved in Crohn's disease.

Option D: On endoscopic examination, discontinuous "skip" lesions are visualized. These are irregular areas of inflamed mucosa that are ulcerated with mucopurulent exudate separated by intervening, normal-appearing intestinal mucosa.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: Which of the following is the earliest sign in Crohn's disease?
questions.explanation:
Aphthous ulcers, surrounded by a rim of erythematous mucosa, are the earliest lesions seen in a patient with Crohn's disease during endoscopy.

Crohn's colitis usually spares the rectum and is most severe in the ileocaecal region.

  • In early Crohn's disease, small, punched-out aphthous ulcers are often seen (the result of submucosal lymphoid follicle expansion).
  • In moderate disease, the aphthous ulcers coalesce into larger ulcers, which may take on the appearance of a star (stellate ulcers).
  • As disease severity increases, submucosal edema and injury can result in cobblestoning of the mucosa (option A) and eventually the formation of serpiginous ulcers, which are typical findings in Crohn's disease. 

Thorn-like extraluminal projections in barium studies are known as rose-thorn appearance, and are a typical sign of Crohn's disease. They represent deep penetrating linear ulcers or fissurings typically seen within stenosed terminal ileum with a thickened wall. (Options C and D)

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: The Van Nuys grading system for ductal carcinoma in situ does not include:
questions.explanation:
Staining for estrogen and progesterone receptors is not part of the Van Nuys system used for grading DCIS. 

The components of the Van Nuys prognostic index (VNPI) are as follows:

  • Size of the tumor
  • Extent of resection margin 
  • Histological variant of DCIS - based on nuclear grade, presence of necrosis, presence of microcalcification
  • Age of the patient

Patients with a high score in this grading system benefit from radiotherapy after excision, whereas those with low-grade and completely excised tumors, need no further treatment.

A score ranging from 1 (lesions with the best prognosis) to 3 (lesions with the worst prognosis) is given for each of the four prognostic predictors. Total scores range from 4 (least likely to recur) to 12 (most likely to recur).

Silverstein Van Nuys prognostic index for DCIS
Parameters Score 1 Score 2 Score 3
Size(mm) ≤15 16-40 ≥41
Margin(mm) ≥10 1-9 <1
Class Grade 1 or 2 without necrosis Grade 1 or 2 with necrosis Grade 3 with or without necrosis
Age(years) >60 40-60 <40
  • Scores 4-7 with >3mm margin: Excision alone 
  • Score 7 with < 3 mm margin, score 8 with > 3mm margin, score 9 with >5mm margin: Excision with RT
  • Score 9 with < 5mm margin & score 10,11,12: Mastectomy

Note: The type of microcalcification seen on imaging, helps in determining the nuclear grade of DCIS. While the linear branching type of microcalcification is associated with high nuclear grade, fine granular type is associated with low nuclear grade.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: Which of the following statements are true with regards to a keloid scar?
options: The extent does not cross the wound margins
Wide excision of the keloid scar prevents recurrence
Histopathology of a keloid scar shows reduced collagen and increased vascularity
A keloid scar forms due to increase in the level of growth factors
questions.correct_answer: A keloid scar forms due to increase in the level of growth factors
questions.explanation:
Keloid scars are associated with elevated levels of growth factor leading to increased proliferation of fibrous tissue.

A keloid scar is defined as excessive scar tissue that extends beyond the boundaries of the original incision or wound (option A) and rarely regresses on its own.  It is more common in darker-pigmented ethnicities.

It can arise from surgery, burns, skin inflammation, infections, ear piercing, and even spontaneously. It occurs 3 months to years after the initial insult with even minor injuries causing keloid formation.

It most commonly occurs on the skin of the earlobe, deltoid, presternal, upper back, and rarely extends into the subcutaneous tissue.



The histology of keloid scars shows excess collagen and hypervascularity with collagen fibres arranged haphazardly in loose sheets (option C).

Treatment: Keloid scars do not improve spontaneously with time and excision alone has a high rate of recurrence (option B). The following can be done:

  • Pressure - local moulds or elastic garments.
  • Silicone gel sheeting.
  • Intralesional triamcinolone injection.
  • Excision and steroid injections.
  • Excision and postoperative radiation (external beam or brachytherapy).
  • Intralesional excision.
  • Laser to reduce redness.
  • Vitamin E and palm oil massage.


Differences between Keloids and Hypertrophic scars:

questions.question: Which of the following is not true about Barrett's esophagus?
options: It is the intestinal metaplasia of esophagus
Mucus secreting foveolar cells are characteristic
Alician blue is used in the staining of biopsy specimen
It is a reversible cell adaptation
questions.correct_answer: Mucus secreting foveolar cells are characteristic
questions.explanation:
Mucus-secreting goblet cells (not foveolar cells) are characteristic of Barrett's esophagus, as there is intestinal metaplasia of the esophagus. Foveolar cells are the mucus-secreting cells in the stomach.

Barrett's esophagus is a complication of chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and it is estimated to occur in about 10% of individuals with symptomatic GERD. Symptoms include heartburn, regurgitation and sometimes dysphagia. Obese white men over the age of 60 years represent the highest-risk group.

Intestinal metaplasia in the esophagus occurs due to chronic irritation of the esophagus in GERD (option A) since intestinal epithelium is better suited to handling gastric acid exposure. Hence, mucus-secreting goblet cells are characteristic of Barrett's esophagus. Since all metaplasia are reversible, Barrett's esophagus is also reversible (option D). Only 0.2 to 1% of Barrett's esophagus leads to dysplasia and adenocarcinoma.



Alician blue is used in the staining of the biopsy specimen, as it stains the goblet cells (option C). Mucicarmine is the specific stain.

Seattle protocol is used for the management of Barrett's esophagus.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: 3. An elderly male presented with epigastric pain, anorexia, weight loss and jaundice since 2 years. He had scratch marks over the body. On examination, the gall bladder was palpable, smooth and non-tender. Identify the diagnosis.
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of an elderly male presenting with epigastric pain, anorexia, weight loss and jaundice for 2 years with a palpable, smooth and non-tender gall bladder suggests the most probable diagnosis to be carcinoma of the head of the pancreas. Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas presents with jaundice that occurs secondary to obstruction of the distal bile duct. It can also be associated with nausea, epigastric discomfort, weight loss, pruritus, dark urine and pale stools with steatorrhoea. In the absence of jaundice, symptoms are often non-specific, such as vague discomfort, anorexia and weight loss. On examination, there may be evidence of a palpable liver and a palpable gallbladder. According to Courvoisier's Law, in a patient with jaundice, with a palpable, enlarged, non-tender gallbladder, the cause is unlikely to be due to gallstones and is more likely to be due to a periampullary malignancy. This is because the common bile duct obstruction by gallstones would lead to chronic inflammation, which causes the gallbladder to shrink and become fibrotic. The gallbladder is enlarged in conditions causing a slow occlusion, as in tumours surrounding the distal common bile duct, which implicates possible cancer of the head of the pancreas. With widespread disease, a left supraclavicular node (Virchow node) and a periumbilical lymph node (Sister Mary Joseph node) may be palpable. In cases of peritoneal dissemination, perirectal tumour involvement may be palpable through digital rectal examination, known as the Blumer shelf. Other options: Option A: Choledocholithiasis is usually asymptomatic. Symptomatic patients with cholangitis have bouts of pain, jaundice and fever, known as Charcot’s triad.  Option C: Patients with carcinoma of the gall bladder may be asymptomatic. If symptoms are present, they are usually indistinguishable from those of benign gallbladder disease, such as biliary colic or cholecystitis, particularly in older patients. Jaundice, palpable mass and anorexia are late features. Option D: Hepatocellular carcinoma is most commonly seen in men 50 to 60 years of age who complain of right upper quadrant abdominal pain, weight loss and have a palpable mass. Presentation at an advanced stage is often with vague right upper quadrant abdominal pain that sometimes radiates to the right shoulder. Other nonspecific symptoms that can be seen are anorexia, nausea, lethargy, and weight loss.

questions.question: 6. A malignant neck swelling was surgically removed from a patient, shown in the image below. What will the patient likely present with 2-3 days after the procedure?
questions.explanation:
The given image suggests total thyroidectomy, and the patient is likely to present with carpopedal spasm 2-3 days after the procedure. Thyroid surgery, particularly total thyroidectomy with a concomitant central neck dissection, is the most common cause of hypoparathyroidism. There is transient hypocalcemia due to ischemia of the parathyroid glands, but permanent hypoparathyroidism is rare. Hypoparathyroidism can also occur after parathyroid surgery. Hypoparathyroidism results in hypocalcemia. Acute hypocalcemia leads to decreased ionised calcium and increased neuromuscular excitability. Patients initially experience numbness in the circumoral and fingertip areas along with a tingling sensation.  Other symptoms and signs of hypocalcemia: * Chvostek sign: contraction of facial muscles that is elicited by tapping on the facial nerve anterior to the ear * Trousseau's sign: carpopedal spasm that is elicited by occluding blood flow to the forearm with a blood pressure cuff for 2–3 minutes * Mental symptoms like anxiety, confusion, and depression * Laryngeal stridor * Convulsions Intravenous calcium infusion is rarely required and most patients with post-operative hypocalcemia can be treated with oral calcium and vitamin D supplements.  Other options: Option A: Deviation of the angle of the mouth is seen in injury of the marginal mandibular nerve and facial nerve palsy.  Option B: Hoarseness of voice occurs in laryngeal disorders like tumours and recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy. Option D: Migratory thrombophlebitis occurs in vascular diseases such as Buerger's disease.

questions.question: 9. The following image depicting bile duct injury shows which type of Strasberg classification?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows a bile leak from the cystic duct stump and a minor biliary radicle in the gallbladder fossa. According to Strasberg’s classification, the image given belongs to type A bile duct injury. Biliary injury may occur post-laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The most common site of bile leak following cholecystectomy is the cystic duct. The Strasberg classification of bile duct injury is a widely used system to anatomically define these injuries by location: * Type A: Bile leak from the cystic duct stump or a minor biliary radicle in the gallbladder fossa * Type B: Occluded right posterior sectoral duct * Type C: Bile leak from the divided right posterior sectoral duct * Type D: Bile leak from the main bile duct without major tissue loss * Type E: Injury to the main hepatic duct; classified according to the level of injury * E1: Transected main bile duct with a stricture more than 2cm from the hilus * E2: Transected main bile duct with a stricture less than 2cm from the hilus * E3: Stricture of the hilus with right and left ducts in communication * E4: Stricture of the hilus with separation of right and left hepatic ducts * E5: Stricture of the right aberrant sectoral duct and the main bile duct MRCP is the gold standard for evaluating the biliary tree's morphology completely. MRCP with magnetic resonance angiography is more useful in cases of associated vascular injury. An HIDA scan can confirm the presence of a bile leak or biliary obstruction.  For an unstable patient, temporary external biliary drainage is achieved by passing a catheter percutaneously into an intrahepatic duct. When the condition improves, definitive surgery can be undertaken. The main principle of surgery is to maintain the duct length and the restoration of biliary drainage.

questions.question: 11. A 30 year old female underwent the procedure shown in the image following a burn injury. Which statement is true regarding this procedure?

The burn has a tourniquet-like effect, which can lead to a compromise in respiration (torso) and peripheral circulation (limbs). The tourniquet effect of this injury is treated by incising the whole length of full-thickness burns. For the chest, two longitudinal and two horizontal incisions are made. There should be evidence of immediate improvement of respiration and, if intubated, the ventilation pressures after performing escharotomy. For the limbs, the escharotomy incision is performed in the midaxial line to avoid major nerves. An escharotomy can cause significant blood loss, and hence, the use of cutting diathermy and appropriate dressings must be considered along with the availability of blood for transfusion. questions.question: 13. A 42-year-old woman had a non-specific right upper quadrant pain. The gross section of the excised tumor is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given history of non-specific right upper quadrant pain, with the given gross specimen showing a well-circumscribed lesion with a central stellate scar, is suggestive of focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH). FNH is the second most common benign tumor of the liver after hemangioma. It is commonly seen in young women. It is believed to be a hyperplastic response to an anomalous artery. Patients are mostly asymptomatic, and FNH is often an incidental finding. If symptoms are noted, vague abdominal pain is the most common symptom. On histological examination, cords of hepatocytes are seen with atypical biliary epithelium scattered throughout.  Contrast-enhanced CT is diagnostic for focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH). It appears as a well-circumscribed lesion with a central stellate scar containing a large artery branching out in a spoke-wheel pattern. It shows intense homogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase, and it is isodense as compared to the background liver in the venous phase. The contrast-enhanced CT image of focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) is shown below.

Due to the presence of Kupffer cells, FNH appears as a hotspot on a Tc 99m sulfur colloid scan. These tumors do not have the risk of malignant transformation; therefore, asymptomatic patients do not require treatment. Careful observation of symptomatic FNH with serial imaging is reasonable, as symptoms may resolve in a significant number of cases. Patients with persistent symptomatic FNH or an enlarging mass should be considered for resection. Another tumor that can show a central stellate scar is renal oncocytoma. Other options: Option A: Metastatic tumor is the most common tumor of the liver. It typically presents as multiple nodular masses leading to hepatomegaly, and these nodules may replace large areas of liver parenchyma. Occasionally, metastatic lesions can appear as a solitary nodule. Option C: Hepatic adenoma is a well-defined, discrete liver mass that may sometimes be multiple. It is often associated with hemorrhage and carries a risk of rupture, which can lead to massive abdominal bleeding. Option D: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary malignant tumor of the liver. It may present as a single large mass or diffusely infiltrate the entire liver. The lipid-rich clear cell variant of HCC shows abundant fat and glycogen in tumor cells. The external surface of the tumor is usually nodular or congested with a tan appearance, while the cut surface is solid and variegated, with areas of cystic change. questions.question: 14. A 45-year-old male presented with difficulty in swallowing and weight loss. The barium swallow gives the following finding along with bronchectatic changes on chest X ray. What is the investigation of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario, along with the barium swallow showing a bird beak appearance, is suggestive of achalasia cardia. Manometry is the investigation of choice. Pearl PM1528: Achalasia Cardia Achalasia cardia is a rare disease caused by the loss of ganglion cells within the esophageal myenteric plexus. Their absence leads to increased tone of the lower esophageal sphincter, impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), and absent peristalsis. Achalasia is the only true motility disorder of the esophagus. * Primary achalasia is due to ganglion cell degeneration and is thought to be due to an autoimmune process attributable to latent infection with human herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1) combined with genetic susceptibility. * Secondary achalasia may arise in Chaga's disease. Clinical features: * Dysphagia (solid and liquid food) * Regurgitation * Chest pain * Weight loss * Bronchitis, pneumonia, or lung abscess from aspiration Differential diagnosis: Diffuse esophageal spasm, pseudoachalasia On barium swallow: Bird beak-appearance Investigation of choice: Manometry (most sensitive) Treatment: Pneumatic dilatation, Heller myotomy

Pearl PM2445: Barium swallow Diffuse esophageal spasm: Corkscrew appearance

Feline esophagus: Transient transverse bands seen in the mid and lower esophagus on a double-contrast barium swallow. It is seen in active gastroesophageal reflux, hiatus hernia, and eosinophilic esophagitis.

Achalasia: Dilated esophagus with a retained column of barium and bird beak sign.

Zenker's diverticulum: Posterior outpouching of the hypopharynx through a weakness in the muscle layer called Killian dehiscence.

Esophageal carcinoma: Irregular narrowing, mucosal destruction, and shouldered margins.

Schatzki's ring: Thin submucosal circumferential ring in the lower esophagus at the squamocolumnar junction.

Esophageal web in a patient with Plummer Vinson syndrome. Esophageal webs are thin membranes of normal esophageal tissue consisting of mucosa and submucosa. Translucent part denotes esophageal web.



Esophageal leiomyoma is the most common benign tumor of the esophagus. On barium swallow, it is seen as a discrete ovoid mass that is well outlined by barium (smooth submucosal mass). Its borders form slightly obtuse angles with the esophagal wall. The image below depicts a barium study showing the classic semilunar filling defect.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: 15. A patient with hypertensive episodes, with an MRI abdomen showing a suprarenal mass, is planned for surgery. 24-hour urine shows metanephrine levels to be elevated. What drug will be given preoperatively and also intraoperatively?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario suggests the diagnosis to be Pheochromocytoma. The drug that will be given preoperatively and also intraoperatively is Nicardipine. The medical management of pheochromocytomas requires blood pressure control and volume repletion. Nicardipine is a calcium channel blocker that is commonly used preoperatively. It inhibits norepinephrine-mediated calcium transport into vascular smooth muscle. Nicardipine also helps to control blood pressure intraoperatively. Calcium channel blockers are indicated in patients who are not able to tolerate alpha blockade because of profound orthostasis or for those patients who need additional blood pressure control. It is as effective as alpha and beta blockers, both preoperatively and intraoperatively.  Preoperatively, blood pressure control is primarily with alpha blockers. Irreversible, long-acting α-blockers such as phenoxybenzamine are started 1 to 3 weeks before surgery. Selective alpha-blockers such as prazosin, doxazosin, and terazosin can also be used. Beta-blockers such as propranolol can be added preoperatively in patients who have persistent tachycardia and arrhythmias. Beta-blockers should be given after adequate alpha-blockade and hydration to avoid the effects of unopposed alpha stimulation, such as hypertensive crisis and congestive heart failure. Nicardipine, Nitroprusside, Nitroglycerin, and Phentolamine are used for intraoperative control of blood pressure. Esmolol can be administered to control heart rate. Other options: Option B: Esmolol is a short-acting beta-blocker that can be used to manage intraoperative arrhythmias. Option C: Clonidine is an alpha-agonist that suppresses neurogenically mediated catecholamine excess but not secretion from pheochromocytomas. Option D: Phenoxybenzamine is a long-acting α-blocker that is given preoperatively, usually 1 to 3 weeks before surgery. Pearl PM1140: Clinical features of Pheochromocytoma (By frequency of occurrence) * Classical triad of symptoms: * Headaches – most common symptom * Profuse sweating * Palpitations and tachycardia * Hypertension (sustained or intermittent) – most common sign * Anxiety, panic attacks * Hyperglycemia * Hypercalcemia * Pallor - due to alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction * Polyuria and polydipsia  * Orthostatic hypotension * Dilated cardiomyopathy * Erythrocytosis, high hematocrit (hemoconcentration) * Constipation * Abdominal pain * Weakness * Weight loss * Nausea Pearl PM0788: Pheochromocytoma Features: * When pheochromocytoma is associated with the MEN syndrome it is rarely malignant. * Phaeochromocytomas are greyish-pink on the cut surface and are usually highly vascularised. * Zellbalen cells and nuclei with salt and pepper chromatin are seen. Factors indicating more chances of malignancy: * An increased PASS (phaeochromocytoma of the adrenal gland scale score) * High number of Ki-67-positive cells * Vascular invasion or a breached capsule Diagnosis: * Measurement of the plasma metanephrines is the most sensitive screening test. * MRI is the IOC. * Biopsy and CT Contrast scans are contraindicated in order to avoid a hypertensive crisis. Treatment: * Adrenalectomy is preferred TOC. * Size<5 cm -  Laparoscopic adrenalectomy * Preop Alpha blockers should be given

questions.question: 16. A patient presented with odynophagia and cervical lymphadenitis. On examination, an ulcerated growth was present on the base of the tongue, which was found to be squamous cell carcinoma. What is the most common organism associated?
questions.explanation:
HPV is the most common organism associated with squamous cell carcinoma. In the oropharynx, most of the squamous cell carcinomas (SCC), particularly those involving the tonsils, the base of the tongue, and the pharynx, occur due to oncogenic variants of HPV. Early detection of HPV-associated head and neck SCC can be delayed because the anatomic sites of origin (tonsillar crypts, base of tongue, and oropharynx) are not readily accessible for cytologic screening (unlike the cervix) for premalignant lesions. The presenting features of oropharyngeal SCC include multiple large cystic cervical lymph nodes with a small primary lesion. Early-stage tumours may be cured by transoral laser surgery, transoral robotic surgery or radiotherapy. Intermediate- or late-stage disease is usually managed with concurrent chemoradiotherapy or with open surgery and reconstruction using myocutaneous pedicles or free flaps. Larger lesions with recurrences require open surgery and reconstruction. Neck dissection is required in most cases where surgery is the primary treatment modality and is also required for patients who have only partially responded following chemoradiotherapy. questions.question: 17. A 25-year-old following a RTA with head injury was brought to the ER, and a CT scan showed normal findings, but the patient died within 3 hours. Autopsy showed petechial hemorrhages in the corpus callosum, focal lesions in the brain stem, and retraction ball appearance in the internal capsule. What is the cause?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with a normal CT and the given autopsy findings are probably due to a diffuse axonal injury. A diffuse axonal injury is a form of primary brain injury seen in high-energy accidents. It is caused by damage to axons throughout the brain due to rotational acceleration and then deceleration. Axons may be completely disrupted and then retract, forming axon balls. Small hemorrhages can be seen in more severe cases, especially on MRI (investigation of choice). Hemorrhage is classically seen in the corpus callosum and the dorsolateral midbrain. The prognosis is very poor. MRI showing multiple hypointense punctate foci within the subcortical and deep white matter within the corpus callosum is characteristic of diffuse axonal injury.

Pearl PM2128: Diffuse Axonal Injury The mechanism of diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is primarily a non-impact rotational acceleration-deceleration injury. This leads to the deformation of the axons by stretching them. Pathology of DAI: * Changes in permeability of the axolemma * Axonal swelling * Intracellular calcium accumulation * Proteolysis * The collapse of the cytoskeleton * 'Retraction balls or globes' - bulbous and clubbed axons. Seen earliest at 12-18 hours. The number of retraction balls begins to decrease after 2-3 weeks after injury and a cluster of microglial cells appears followed by astrocytosis and demyelination. * Immuno-histochemistry shows beta-amyloid precursor protein - the most reliable indicator of axon damage. Seen earliest at 2-3 hours.  Image shows scattered axonal retraction balls stained with Congo Red:

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the flap given in the image.
options: Pedicled TRAM based on superior epigastric artery
Free TRAM based on superior and inferior epigastric artery
DIEP based on deep inferior epigastric artery
Lower Abdominal Fat based inferior epigastric vessels
questions.correct_answer: DIEP based on deep inferior epigastric artery
questions.explanation:
The given image showing only skin and fat moved to the chest is suggestive of a deep inferior epigastric artery perforator flap (DIEP), based on the deep inferior epigastric artery.

DIEP is a variant of TRAM flap and free flap where only the skin and fat are moved to the chest. A microvascular technique is used in which no muscle is taken and the perforating vessels are dissected out.

As the muscle is spared in DIEP, there is a reduced risk of abdominal wall weakness and its associated complications. 

Other options: 

Options A and B: The pedicled TRAM flap is based on the superior epigastric artery and the free TRAM flap is based on superior and inferior epigastric arteries (supercharged TRAM flap); however, the given image depicts a deep inferior epigastric artery flap. In TRAM flaps: 

  • The skin, fat, and muscle are moved to the chest.
  • It provides good cosmesis and bulk since it has a soft tissue consistency similar to the breast.
  • Disadvantages include epigastric bulge, partial flap loss, fat necrosis, abdominal wall weakness, and hernias.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: What is the most common site of gastrinoma in MEN 1 syndrome?
questions.explanation:
The most common site of gastrinoma in MEN 1 syndrome is the duodenum.

Gastrinoma is the most common pancreatic islet tumor in MEN 1 syndrome, arising from the G cells of the pancreas. Gastrinoma, associated with marked gastric acid production and recurrent peptic ulcers, is called Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. The majority of gastrinomas occur in the gastrinoma (Passaro's) triangle.

In MEN 1, they often occur in patients <30 years. Patients present with abdominal pain (the most common symptom), diarrhea and steatorrhea. 

Management: 

  • Medical management for tumors <2 cm with proton-pump inhibitors. 
  • Surgery for tumors >2 cm.
  • Proton-pump inhibitors with somatostatin analogues for advanced locoregional disease or metastasis.

questions.question: A 50-year-old male who is a chronic smoker presented to the hospital with intermittent claudication pain of both thigh and buttock region on walking about 500 m. Which of the following is a likely diagnosis?
options: Arterial disease involving the superficial femoral artery
Arterial disease involving the profunda femoris artery
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of arterial disease with aortoiliac involvement. Classically, the muscle group affected by claudication is one anatomical level below the level of arterial disease.

Intermittent claudication is a feature of chronic arterial disease or occlusion of the artery.  Aortoiliac disease affects the infrarenal aorta and iliac arteries.

Management involves smoking cessation, lifestyle modifications, and treatment of underlying diabetes or hyperlipidemia if present.

For claudication, cilostazol or pentoxyfilline is used. Cilostazol is superior to pentoxyfilline. 

Surgical options include aortoiliac bypass, aortobifemoral bypass, percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA), which can be with or without stent placement, and thromboendarterectomy.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about retrosternal goitre?
options: Operated in all patients regardless of symptoms
Sternal incision is always required to operate
It receives blood supply from the thoracodorsal artery
Most of the retrosternal goitres can be removed by a neck incision
questions.correct_answer: Most of the retrosternal goitres can be removed by a neck incision
questions.explanation:
Most of the retrosternal goiters can be removed by neck incision (transcervical approach).

Retrosternal goitre is defined as having >50% of the goiter below the suprasternal notch. It can be either primary or secondary.

  • Primary: rare and arises from ectopic thyroid tissue in the mediastinum; receives blood supply from intrathoracic blood vessels. It is not related to thyroid tissue in the neck.
  • Secondary: they are the most common type; an extension of enlarged thyroid from the neck, usually arising from the lower pole of nodular goitre. It receives its blood supply from superior and inferior thyroid vessels.

The majority of patients are asymptomatic or have minimal symptoms. If the gland enlarges within the thoracic inlet, the pressure may lead to dysphagia, tracheal compression, and eventually airway symptoms. Pemberton sign can be positive (facial flushing and dilatation of cervical veins upon raising the arms above the head).

CECT neck and thorax is the investigation of choice.

Over 95% of retrosternal goiters can be removed via a transcervical incision since they are an extension from thyroid tissue in the neck.

Other options:

Option A: Surgical removal of the retrosternal goiter is indicated in patients with significant airway compression, and in young patients who have symptoms such as dyspnoea or dysphagia. 

Option B: Median sternotomy approach is indicated in:

  • Primary mediastinal goiter
  • Malignant retrosternal goitre
  • Very large retrosternal goiter
  • Recurrence in the mediastinum

For a primary mediastinal goiter whose boundaries are completely within the chest, resection is often achieved through median sternotomy or thoracotomy to ensure that the vessels supplying the tumor are properly ligated. Removing the tumor through a cervical approach can result in uncontrolled bleeding and is generally avoided. 

Option C: Blood supply to the retrosternal goiter is from the thyroid vessels (secondary retrosternal goiter).

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: An 80-year-old woman presented with complaints of fatigue. On imaging, she was found to have a scleroatrophic gall bladder with impacted stones in it. A large stone was also present in the common bile duct and the biliary tree is dilated. What is the next step in management?
options: Immediately take up patient for cholecystectomy
questions.explanation:
An 80-year-old woman with imaging showing a scleroatrophic gall bladder with impacted stones and a stone in the bile duct is suggestive of chronic cholelithiasis with choledocholithiasis. ERCP is the next line of management for this patient. 

Choledocholithiasis is the presence of stone in the common bile duct (CBD) or biliary tree. It can be primary or secondary:  

  • Primary stones are formed in the CBD or biliary tree itself and are rare.
  • Secondary stones are passed from the gallbladder to the CBD. They are easier to manage than primary stones.

It can be an asymptomatic and incidental finding or present with features such as jaundice (most common), abdominal pain, and fatigue. When there is inflammation of the biliary tree (cholangitis), the patient will have intermittent pain, fever, and jaundice (Charcot's triad). 

Investigations: 

  • Liver function tests will show elevated direct bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase levels. 
  • Abdominal ultrasound is the first imaging modality done and may show gallstones and dilated bile duct (>8 mm). 
  • CT is sensitive for CBD stones. It shows stones, location, ductal stricture or block, ductal dilatation, and intrahepatic biliary changes.
  • MRCP is highly sensitive and specific for CBD stones, but it is only diagnostic and intervention cannot be performed.

Management: 

  • ERCP with sphincterotomy is the procedure of choice, followed by the removal of stones using a dormia basket or placement of a stent.
  • Despite ERCP being an invasive procedure, it has the advantage of being both a diagnostic and therapeutic procedure and is more suited for elderly patients who cannot tolerate anesthesia and surgery.

Other options: 

Option A: Cholecystectomy is not recommended for elderly patients, owing to the risk of old age and associated anesthetic and surgical complications.

Option C: Wait and watch approach can be done for asymptomatic patients, and patients with smaller stones.

Option D: CT is sensitive for CBD stones, but it is only diagnostic and intervention cannot be performed.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: A 35-year-old man presented with recurrent episodes of fever with chills. MRCP image is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The presence of fever and chills, along with the MRCP showing multiple areas of intrahepatic beading is typical of primary sclerosing cholangitis.

Option B: Caroli's disease is a rare congenital condition characterized by irregular dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts with a normal extrahepatic duct system. It is common in both sexes and mostly presents before the age of 30 years with abdominal pain, cholangitis, or end-stage liver disease. MRCP shows irregular, cystic dilation of the large proximal intrahepatic bile ducts with a normal common bile duct. 

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is an autoimmune condition characterized by inflammatory strictures involving the intra and extra-hepatic biliary tree. It is a progressive condition that leads to secondary biliary cirrhosis. 

MRCP or ERCP will show demonstrate multifocal, diffuse dilatation and strictures of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary trees, this pattern is a beading or chain of lakes appearance. Pseudodiverticula of extrahepatic bile ducts are pathognomic of PSC. MRCP is useful in diagnosis and surveillance, while ERCP is reserved for the treatment of dominant strictures and to exclude malignancy. 

The below image shows a cholangiogram of primary sclerosing cholangitis:



The common age group of primary sclerosing cholangitis is 30-45 years. Men are affected twice as commonly as women. Two-thirds of these cases are associated with ulcerative colitis. It is also associated with Riedel’s thyroiditis and retroperitoneal fibrosis. 10–20% of patients develop cholangiocarcinoma.

Clinical features of a patient with PSC include pruritis, fever, chills, right upper quadrant discomfort, jaundice, and weight loss. 

Liver function tests show a cholestatic pattern with an elevation of ALP and GGT and smaller rises in the aminotransferases. Bilirubin values may be variable.

Liver biopsy excludes other causes of cholestatic liver disease and defines the stage of PSC. It shows onion skin concentric periductal fibrosis. With disease progression, periportal fibrosis occurs, progressing to bridging necrosis, and eventually biliary cirrhosis.

Currently, there is no known effective medical therapy. Surgical management involving resection of extrahepatic biliary tree and hepaticojejunostomy has shown reasonable effects. For patients with advanced liver disease, liver transplantation is the only available option.

Other options: 

Option C: Oriental cholangitis, also known as recurrent pyogenic cholangitis is characterized by recurrent attacks of cholangitis due to bile stasis and stone formation. Patients between 30-40 years and both sexes are equally affected. It is caused due to infections (liver flukes, E.coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, and Proteus). Patients present with Charcot's triad (intermittent fever, pain, and jaundice). MRCP shows intra or extrahepatic calculi, dilatation of ducts, and strictures. 

Option D: Biliary carcinoma  (cholangiocarcinoma) most commonly affects patients >60 years and presents with fever, abdominal pain, weight loss, and features of obstructive jaundice. MRCP shows irregular narrowing of the bile duct involved by the tumor, with asymmetric upstream dilatation of the intrahepatic ducts.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: The most common neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas is
questions.explanation:
The most common neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas is insulinoma (4 per million).

Insulinoma is an insulin-producing tumor of the pancreas, with more than 90% of them being benign. It occurs in >40 years in patients without MEN 1 syndrome and <40 years in patients with MEN 1. It presents with symptoms of hypoglycemia such as weakness, headaches, sweating, faintness, seizures, and altered behavior. These occur after fasting or exertion and improve after glucose intake. 

The investigation of choice for insulinoma is the determination of 72-hour fasting glucose and serum insulin levels. C-peptide and proinsulin levels are also elevated.

Medical management includes:

  • Frequent carbohydrate-rich meals
  • Somatostatin analogs like octreotide are effective in controlling symptoms due to excess insulin secretion. They should be used with caution as they can suppress counterregulatory hormones, such as growth hormone (GH), glucagon, and catecholamines, and precipitously worsen hypoglycemia. 
  • Diazoxide can be used in the initial management of insulinoma as it inhibits insulin release. Its side effects include sodium retention and nausea. 
  • Everolimus has been found to be highly effective in improving glycemic control in patients with insulinoma owing to its antitumor effect and induction of insulin resistance.

Enucleation and pancreatectomy are the definitive surgical management of insulinoma.

Other options:

Option A: Gastrinoma has an incidence of 0.5 to 4 in a million.

Options B & D: Somatostatinoma and VIPoma are much rarer than gastrinoma.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: A patient comes with long-standing non-pitting edema in the legs. What is the most probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Lymphedema is the most probable cause of long-standing non-pitting edema in the limbs.

Lymphedema is the abnormal accumulation of protein-rich fluid in the interstitial spaces of the tissues.

Lymphedema can be primary or secondary.

Primary lymphedema includes: 

  • Lymphedema congenita (0-2 years): more common in males, involves multiple limbs, face, and genitalia. It can be familial or sporadic. The familial type is called Nonne Milroy syndrome.
  • Lymphedema praecox (2-35 years): more common in females, the most common type of primary lymphedema with a peak incidence in puberty. It can be familial or sporadic. The familial type is called Meig's disease.
  • Lymphedema tarda (>35 years): Rare and uncommon.

Secondary lymphedema is more common than primary and is the most common cause of lymphedema overall. Causes include lymph node dissection (axillary or inguinal), post-mastectomy, postoperative radiotherapy, obesity, varicose vein surgery, and trauma.

Complications of lymphedema include infections, skin changes, recurent cellulitis, non-healing ulcers, and lymphangiosarcoma.

Treatment mostly includes patient education and nonsurgical interventions, which include limb elevation, and external compressive garments. When the above methods fail, surgery can be considered.

questions.subject: General Surgery
questions.question: A 41-year-old female patient presented with a tortuous swelling over the left side of the scalp and face as shown in the image given below. On local examination, the swelling was pulsatile. On auscultation, a bruit was heard. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The presence of a tortuous, pulsatile swelling over the scalp and face is suggestive of a cirsoid aneurysm.

Cirsoid aneurysm is a slow-growing, tortuous swelling that develops due to abnormal arteriovenous connections among the subcutaneous blood vessels. They are usually congenital. However, in some cases, they may be traumatic. The superficial temporal artery is most commonly involved.



Patients present with a tortuous, pulsatile swelling over the scalp or face. They are usually asymptomatic and present to the clinic due to cosmetic deformity. However, some patients may have headache, tinnitus, and/or bleeding. A loud bruit is heard on auscultation.

Angiography is the investigation of choice.

Treatment includes surgical resection, endovascular occlusion or injection of percutaneous sclerosing agents.
